text: So, we are perceiving something. However, presence means that our perception should be as good as perceiving reality. That means we should not be able to distinguish between our perception of stimuli generated by a computer vis-à-vis our perception of stimuli generated from the real world. So, in other words, we are perceiving that we are already in the real world; nothing changed. That means we are unable to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world; that is presence, or rather, to say, perfect presence. How are these two related: immersion and presence? Immersion can be an objective and quantifiable description of what any particular system can provide or does provide, whereas presence is a state of consciousness or the psychological sense of being in the virtual environment. So, immersion is what the technology gives us. We can measure or we can comprehend what the technology can provide. However, when we are talking about presence, it is inside the user's mind. There is no direct manifestation of it. It is difficult to objectively measure. So, subjective experience has to be taken into account. That is the major difference between these two concepts: immersion and presence. Now, as is probably obvious by now, presence can be a function of both the user, that is the subjective experience, as well as immersion, that is the objective or technological experience. So, immersion aids presence, but it does not mean that if we provide immersive technology, then presence will automatically happen. Immersion is capable of producing presence, but not necessarily always.

text: So, in order to do that, a VR system developer or VR content creator should consider a few things. One is representational fidelity. In the induction of CS when the resolution changed from 1K to 2K. So, when the resolution changed to 2K from 1K, CS induction reduced. However, that reduction was not significant when resolutions were further changed from 2K to 3K and 3K to 4K. That means up to a change of 2K, it is likely to affect the induction of CS. But if we change the resolution beyond that, if we increase the resolution, then it is not likely to change anything related to induction of CS. Another hardware-related factor is latency. Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world. So, you are doing something in the physical world which gets reflected in the virtual world. The delay between these two, the time gap between these two, is called latency. Now, several studies have investigated the relationship between CS and latency. In the context of HMD-based VR experience, HMD or head-mounted display-based VR experience, it is found that sickness increases with latency. The more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce sickness. A related external factor. Another hardware-related external factor is latency jitter. So, latency is the delay between what you do in the physical world and what is happening in the virtual world due to that action.

There is another passive mode; here user activities are recorded or videotaped and So, there is no observer as such, but the activities are recorded and then observed later by the observer. If there are some issues, those can be clarified through interaction with the users. One important thing here is that during the inquiry, the observer should act as an apprentice, and treat the users as masters. So, this is called the master apprentice model. The purpose is to learn the user behavior, not to teach users how to behave. So, it is not easy.

That actually involves real walking.

text: One is full gait technique, partial gait techniques and gait negation techniques. So, these three are the broad categories of walking-based locomotion techniques: full gait, partial gait and gait negation techniques. What happens in full gait techniques? That actually involves real walking. So the user actually walks in the real world and that walk gets translated to virtual movement in the virtual environment, in the immersive environment. Obviously, this is the most natural way to travel. However, as we have seen earlier, giving a completely free form of walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation. Instead, the walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space, which then gets translated to any amount of movement in the potentially infinite virtual space. So, of course, there is a mismatch, although this provides natural form of interaction for navigation as compared to the other techniques. Then comes the second technique, that is partial gait technique. Unlike the previous full gait technique, here partial gait refers to the fact that the user walks but walks in place. That means the user does not actually change the position. As shown in this figure here, as you can see in this animated figure, the user is walking but in a single place. It is not actually moving forward, backward, left, or right. That is the partial gait technique. Now, implementation of these types of techniques may involve walking interfaces, active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors and/or interfaces with pressure sensors and so on. So that depending on the walking behavior, although it may be in a single place, but depending on the behavior of walking in that single place, the pattern can be mapped to different types of walking in the virtual space. So, partial gait techniques require some sort of specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware for providing input.

So, although the user may be moving in multiple directions, the lateral movements in that movement pattern get negated, get canceled because of the specialized setup used and the user or the system maps that movement to a specialized or specific type of virtual movement. So, the user may be walking naturally. However, natural movement involves lateral movement. But to map that type of absolutely natural movements to a particular type of focused movement in the virtual world may be difficult. So, a specialized setup is used to Cancel the lateral movements of the user so that it is easier for the system to understand the user's intention and accordingly perform the navigation in the virtual world. text: So, we should be able to create them rapidly and easily. If these conditions are not met, then the throwaway prototypes working with them becomes quite expensive as is obvious. Next is the incremental prototypes. In this case, the system is designed into units or modules. Each unit is separately prototyped and tested and afterwards it is integrated into the overall system. So, that is incremental prototypes. Finally, we have evolutionary prototypes. In this case, the whole system is prototyped and tested. So, in the case of incremental, we have divided the system into modules based on the system design and each module is separately prototyped, tested, and then they are put together to come up with the whole system. In the case of evolutionary prototypes, we start with the simpler version of the system, test it, refine it, then add more functionalities and in that way we evolve the prototype into the full system. So, based on the testing results, the prototype can be altered and eventually it becomes the final product. So, it is not that separate different modules are prototyped and combined together; it is the whole system from the very beginning. So, those are different ways prototypes can be used. So, we have covered different categories of prototypes, different building approaches, and different ways prototypes can be used. So, now we will be talking about early evaluation or quick evaluation of the prototypes. The basic idea is that these evaluation techniques are used for quick and cheap evaluation. That is, we are not going to spend too much time or too many resources on evaluating our prototype. Typically, a robust evaluation technique involves recruitment of suitably skilled evaluators, some sort of resources, building of a setup for evaluation, and all these things require some resources. Whereas the idea of quick evaluation or expert evaluation is to do the evaluation at an early stage of the design without spending too much time or resources. So, they are typically done at the early stages of design, as you can see from the interactive system development life cycle. Now, in order to perform the quick and cheap evaluation, we require two things. First is at least a low-fidelity prototype; that is, higher quality prototypes are better, but at least we require a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators. Of course, that is quite obvious because without evaluators, we cannot evaluate anything. Now, this evaluation team is unique.

text: First is at least a low-fidelity prototype; that is, higher quality prototypes are better, but at least we require a low-fidelity prototype and a team of evaluators. Of course, that is quite obvious because without evaluators, we cannot evaluate anything. Now, this evaluation team is unique. It may be the design team itself or may include other skilled designers who have some knowledge and skill in the domain of the problem. Optionally, few end users may also be included. Note that here we are testing usability. The primary condition of usability testing is that we must involve the users. However, in the curious case of quick evaluation, Involvement of end users may be optional. Primarily we engage design team members or people familiar with the design problem as evaluators. Why so? Because we are assuming that they are the experts in the domain of the problem and they have as good experience as a user. So their feedback is likely to reflect that of the users. Now since identifying And engaging design team members is much, much less complicated as compared to engaging a full-fledged evaluation team involving end users. So, it is likely to be quick and cheap. Now, the evaluation team should have at least three to five members. More is, of course, always welcome, but three to five should be sufficient. Now, each team member evaluates individually and produces a report. So, the prototype is presented to each evaluator, each evaluator evaluates it independently and produces a report. The report contains a list of usability issues as perceived by the evaluator. At the end, all these reports are combined to produce a final list of usability issues. Now, this combination, of course, is done by the design team, or the lead of the team. There are different ways to perform this quick evaluation. Let us learn two of such expert evaluation techniques. The first technique is called cognitive walkthrough. Now, this is a usability inspection method. Essentially, we identify usability problems by inspecting the prototype.

text: There are different ways to perform this quick evaluation. Let us learn two of such expert evaluation techniques. The first technique is called cognitive walkthrough. Now, this is a usability inspection method. Essentially, we identify usability problems by inspecting the prototype. The requirements for performing a cognitive walkthrough is at least a low-fidelity prototype with support for several tasks. So, essentially that refers to a vertical prototype, whether built using low-fidelity approach or medium-fidelity approach. High-fidelity approach, of course, is more welcome; however, that involves time and cost. So, we require at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a 3 to 5 member team as discussed earlier, and with that we can perform the evaluation. Now, let us try to understand the evaluation technique in terms of an example. So, first we have to make a prototype. So, let us consider a simple calendar application. In our application, we show only months on the first screen. Once a user selects a month, another screen appears showing dates in that month. A user can select any date and add some note. What are the tasks that a user can do with this interface? First, let us identify the tasks. There can be many tasks that can be done. Some of those are selection of a month, selection of a day of a month, addition of some note, getting back to month view from the day view and so on. Now, to perform the cognitive walkthrough, we should make a prototype that supports more than one of these tasks. We can make, as we have seen earlier during our discussion on low-fidelity prototypes, simple paper prototypes for these tasks using the storyboarding approach to support more than one task. Each prototype is a series of sketches depicting changes of screen after each interaction. So essentially, each prototype is a storyboard. Then for the evaluators, we have to create a scenario to perform the tasks supported in the prototype.

text: Each prototype is a series of sketches depicting changes of screen after each interaction. So essentially, each prototype is a storyboard. Then for the evaluators, we have to create a scenario to perform the tasks supported in the prototype. For example, in this case, we can create a scenario such as: you are planning to take a lecture on extended reality You wish to schedule a class on the first Monday of next month. Students are available only on specific Mondays. On other days, they do not have any free slots. They are engaged in some other activities. You want to find out the date so that you can inform students about the class. And you want to find that out using the calendar app. That is a task description or a scenario that you have to create for the prototype to be evaluated by the evaluators. So the task here is to identify the date on which the first Monday of next month falls. And when we convert these two interface-level tasks, that is the things that we need to do to identify, to find out this information from the calendar app, what are the interface-level tasks we need to do? Select next month, locate first Monday, and mark the date. So, these are interface-level tasks. Then what do we do? The procedure says that we give the scenario to the evaluators. The evaluators are asked to find out the date by performing the interface-level tasks with the prototype. Along with that, there are some additional requirements, that is, framing of some questions. So we also need to frame a set of questions which reflect usability issues beforehand. Evaluators report on these issues while they perform the tasks. Some of those example questions with respect to our specific example application can be: Are you able to locate the month you are looking for easily? Is the interaction required to change from month view to day view apparent? Did you find it difficult to locate the first Monday?

text: Some of those example questions with respect to our specific example application can be: Are you able to locate the month you are looking for easily? Is the interaction required to change from month view to day view apparent? Did you find it difficult to locate the first Monday? Was the date clearly visible along with the day? Did you try to go back to the month view? Was the mechanism to go back clearly visible? So what is the purpose of these questions? The purpose is to identify problems users are likely to face. And these are a kind of guideline using which the evaluators can see from a user's point of view whether how easy are these questions to answer, how easy it is to answer these questions, in what way these questions can be answered. However, the evaluators are not expected to answer only yes or no. They should give detailed report on what they felt about the interfaces and interaction with respect to each question. That is, if they face difficulty, where exactly, why they think that difficulty is there and so on. So, not a simple yes or no type answer, but a detailed report. Now, the feedbacks from the evaluators that are received in the form of a report are analyzed to identify the broader usability issues. That is, of course, at the end of the evaluation session. So, all feedbacks from the evaluators are collected and then they are combined, compiled together and broader issues are identified. So, that is cognitive walkthrough. Another technique is heuristic evaluation. So, here the basic idea is to evaluate a system with a checklist. In earlier cases, we have evaluated based on a scenario, task description, and a set of questionnaires. Here, no such scenario or task description is required. Instead, we can evaluate whatever prototype is presented to us, that means the evaluators use a checklist. Items in the checklist are called heuristics.

text: In earlier cases, we have evaluated based on a scenario, task description, and a set of questionnaires. Here, no such scenario or task description is required. Instead, we can evaluate whatever prototype is presented to us, that means the evaluators use a checklist. Items in the checklist are called heuristics. So, here the basic idea is that we perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than task-specific evaluation. So, no need to create scenarios and ask evaluators to perform tasks. Instead, evaluators tick items on a checklist of features of the system as a whole. There are many such checklists available for evaluating interfaces. Some are detailed and system-specific. Some are more focused on broader principles of usability. The latter category contains fewer heuristics because they are broader in nature, not specific to any particular interface. So one such, General set of heuristics is Nielsen's 10 heuristics. It is quite popular and was proposed way back in 1994, primarily related to GUIs. However, they are equally applicable to most interactive systems, for most interactive systems. So, what are those 10 heuristics? Heuristic number 1. Visibility of system status: how visible the status of the system is to the user. Then two is match between system and the real world. So whatever we do on the system, how closely it matches with our experience in the real world. Heuristic three: user control and freedom, whether the user is getting the freedom to do whatever they want to do and what kind of controls are provided to the user. Heuristic four. Consistency and standards: whether the elements, layout, whatever is shown are consistent across different screens and also standards are followed. Heuristic five is error prevention: whether the design helps the user prevent errors. Heuristic six: recognition rather than recall. That means in order to perform a task, whether the user is forced to remember things rather than recognize from some element what to do. Note that recollection is always difficult as compared to recognition of certain activities.

text: Heuristic six: recognition rather than recall. That means in order to perform a task, whether the user is forced to remember things rather than recognize from some element what to do. Note that recollection is always difficult as compared to recognition of certain activities. For example, just by looking at a button, we know that it needs to be pressed. However, if the button is not presented in a 3D mode, a 3D shape, Then it is difficult to recognize just from the shape whether it needs to be pressed or something else needs to be done. In that case, the user has to recall what to do with the button from previous usage of similar systems. So, if the shape is not properly there, then the user will be forced to recall, which is not a good practice. Heuristic 7 is flexibility and efficiency of use. Heuristic 8 says aesthetic and minimalist design. The design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing. Heuristic 9: help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors. Help users recover from errors; that is the main message. And the last, 10th heuristic, is help and documentation. So, for any system, there must be some help and documentation support provided. So, these 10 heuristics can be used for identifying usability problems at an early stage of the design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes. So, what we need to do is low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes. However, vertical prototypes can also be there, but unlike the walkthrough method here. We do not require a vertical prototype mandatorily. It is optional. But in the case of the walkthrough method, a vertical prototype must be there. We also need a team of evaluators with a similar team size, that is at least three to five members. They can be members of design teams or other skilled designers. So they can be designers or other expert designers, not necessarily involved in the design team.

text: We also need a team of evaluators with a similar team size, that is at least three to five members. They can be members of design teams or other skilled designers. So they can be designers or other expert designers, not necessarily involved in the design team. Here, the evaluation process is slightly different as compared to the cognitive walkthrough method. As we have noted, a task scenario is not required. Each evaluator checks the design, that is the prototype, with respect to the heuristics and reports their findings. Reports are combined to determine which heuristics are violated. So, each evaluator is given the prototype and the checklist, that is the heuristics; against each heuristic in the list, the evaluator evaluates and indicates whether the heuristic is followed or violated; if violated, what are the reasons. So, one kind of some sort of commentary on the conformity or violation of the heuristic and for all the heuristics in the list, such a report is prepared by each evaluator, then all the evaluators' reports are combined, compiled, and major issues are identified. So, that is the heuristic evaluation technique. So, with that, we have come to the end of this part of the lecture. So, in summary, we have covered so far the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. text: However, there are two major points of concern. The first issue is that when we collect user feedback on a rating scale, we collect ratings on items. One is after every task is performed, and the second is at the end of the session where all the tasks are performed. So, when should we collect the data? Of course, it is desirable to collect data at both points if feasible. Otherwise, we have to choose either of these two points. Now, depending on when we are collecting the data, we have to create suitable questionnaires. So, corresponding questionnaires may not be the same. So, questionnaires required to collect data after every task need not be the same as the questionnaires required to collect data after the whole session. So, depending on these different requirements, we can have different questionnaires. Already, there are well-known questionnaires. available which can be directly used. text: That is a 5-point agreement scale where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree. In the ASQ questionnaire, the rating scale was 1 to 7. Here it is 1 to 5. Now, how to use the rating? Earlier we saw that we can use the rating for ASQ, that is, the post-task questionnaire, by just taking the average either question-wise or with all three statements taken together. Here it is a little bit different. Here, what we can do is we can combine the ratings for all 10 statements to obtain an overall SUS score using the formula S, that is the score, equals the summation of ri minus 1 plus the summation of 5 minus ri; this whole thing is multiplied by 2.5, where ri is the rating for the ith statement, and i ranges from 1 to 10. So, when i is taking the values of the positive statements, that is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, the expression is ri minus 1, so rating minus 1, and when it is the negative statements, That is 2, 4, 6, 8, 9. Then we use the expression 5 minus R i. Then we add these two weighted sums, add these two sums, and then multiply it with 2.5. That is the formulation to combine the scores. We can interpret the score as a percentage. So, whatever result we get after doing this calculation, we can convert it to a percentage directly. Typically, a SUS score around 70 percent or higher is desirable. So, we can assume that if the score is 70 percent or higher, then the interface is usable. If it is below 70 percent, scores lower than that 70 percent might indicate usability problems. So, we may need to have a re-look at the design. Unlike the expert evaluation technique, as you can see here, the scores do not give a detailed report because it is coming from the users. Users themselves may not know the reason for their satisfaction or dissatisfaction.
